# Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments *Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`ValueVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt), [`ImagingVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt), [`plotly.kt`](reference/visualization.md#plotly-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).* Field has many ways to show a value, and the quickest takes two keystrokes: put `.h` on the end of an expression and run the line. What comes back can land in several places. Some visuals appear **inline in the editor**, beside the line you ran. Some fill an **output area** under the box. Some output areas become **inspectors**, or **little control panels** whose sliders you drag while the code around them keeps running. And helpers like `.h` and `.h2` are about turning an arbitrary Kotlin value into something formatted well enough to read. This page is a tour of the whole family. ## The value visualizer: what `.h` draws Most environments answer "what is this value?" with a line of `toString()`. Field answers with a *picture*: whenever you ask Field to show a value, the **value visualizer** turns it into a compact HTML view — a reflective tree for arbitrary objects, and, for the types Field draws with, a little inline graphic. You reach it three ways, all of which call the same renderer (`ValueVisualizer.visualize(...)`, in `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ValueVisualizer.kt`): ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static value.h // the .h extension: value -> pretty HTML display("inspect", value.h) // drop that HTML into a named output channel box.viz(value = value) // convenience: visualize into the box's "viz" channel ``` `.h` is the lightweight view used throughout Field; its heavier sibling `.h2` opens a paged browser for large structures. The built-in and reflective paths are forgiving: they track recursion by reference, cap depth and preview sizes, catch reflective getter failures, and guard optional plots and thumbnails (including a throwing `Fn.evalFn`). Objects implementing `ToHTML` and callbacks registered with `registerValuePrinter` are extension points whose returned HTML is trusted. `registerValuePrinter` is how a **third-party** type joins in without knowing Field exists, and the worked example is a Kotlin DataFrame: a frame, a column, a row and a `GroupBy` all render as ordinary Field tables, and `.h2` pages a million-row frame through the same offset machinery this page's `.h2` uses everywhere else. See [DataFrames in a Box](dataframe.md#looking-at-a-frame). ### The reflective tree Give the visualizer an ordinary object — a data class, a map, anything with readable properties — and it walks the members into an indented tree. Numbers, booleans, strings, and nested values are each rendered by the same rules, recursively. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static data class Camera( val position: Vector3f, val fieldOfView: Double, val active: Boolean, val layers: List, ) val cam = Camera(Vector3f(0f, 1.5f, -4f), 55.0, true, ["dots", "lines", "labels"]) cam.h ``` ![Reflective tree for a Camera data class](assets/value_visualizers/reflective_tree.png){ width="516" } Notice that the tree is not flat text: the nested `position` is itself rendered as a `vec3`, and `layers` collapses to a list with a size count. The renderer keeps only a handful of fields inline (with a "… +N more fields" expander for the rest) so a large object never floods the output. ### Numeric collections, with stats Arrays and lists of numbers get a preview plus a one-line statistical summary — mean, standard deviation, and range — so you can judge a buffer without scrolling through it. Long collections elide the middle: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val samples = DoubleArray(48) { i -> sin(i / 48.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI) } samples.h ``` ![DoubleArray preview with mean, sigma and range](assets/value_visualizers/double_array.png) The tail reads `… +28 more items [μ=8.90e-17, σ=0.707, range=−1…1] (48)`: the sampled sine averages to ~0, has the expected 0.707 RMS spread, and spans −1…1 — visible immediately, without a plot. The same treatment applies to `IntArray`, `FloatArray`, and numeric `List`s. ### Vectors, matrices, and quaternions Field's generated linear-algebra types render as compact, colour-coded tokens rather than as reflective trees — the point of a `vec3` is its three numbers, not its class internals: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static [vec(0.5, 1.5), vec(1.0, 2.0, 3.0), vec(0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0)].h ``` ![vec2, vec3 and vec4 rendered as compact tokens](assets/value_visualizers/vectors.png){ width="324" } Matrices summarise rather than dump every cell: a `mat3` shows its determinant, a `mat4` shows determinant plus extracted translation, and a quaternion shows its four components. Here they are keyed by a map, which the visualizer renders as a tree — a good way to label several related values at once: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static linkedMapOf( "scale (mat3)" to Matrix3f().set(2f, 0f, 0f, 0f, 3f, 0f, 0f, 0f, 1f), "translate (mat4)" to Matrix4f().identity().apply { set(3, 0, 5f) set(3, 1, -2f) set(3, 2, 1f) }, "spin (quat)" to Quaternionf().rotateY(0.6f), ) .h ``` ![A map of mat3, mat4 and quaternion values](assets/value_visualizers/linalg_map.png){ width="564" } The `mat3` reports `det=6` (2 × 3 × 1), the `mat4` reports `det=1, t=(5, -2, 1)`, and the quaternion shows its normalized components. For the algebra behind these types, see [Linear Algebra](linear_algebra.md). ### An `FLine`, drawn An [`FLine`](fline_examples.md) — Field's core drawable path — is where the renderer stops summarising and starts *drawing*. Alongside its node counts, bounding box, length, and a compressed path signature, it appends a small inline SVG thumbnail of the actual geometry: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val spiral = FLine() val steps = 140 spiral.breakNext() for (i in 0..steps) { val t = i.toDouble() / steps val a = t * 5.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI val r = 8.0 + t * 60.0 val x = 80.0 + Math.cos(a) * r val y = 80.0 + Math.sin(a) * r spiral.lineTo(x, y) } spiral.h ``` ![FLine node stats, path signature, and an SVG spiral thumbnail](assets/value_visualizers/fline_spiral.png){ width="552" } The header reads `FLine (141 nodes)`, then `M=1 L=140 C=0 · b=130×124 · len=1.19e+03`, then the run-compressed signature `M(Lx41) … (Lx22)`, and finally the thumbnail. The thumbnail is normalised into its box and only rendered for paths under a complexity budget, so pasting a huge path into a value view never becomes a rendering hazard. ### An `Fn`, plotted The richest case is a [`Functions.Fn`](functions_examples.md). Field keeps the full reflective tree — its `domain`, `evalFn`, `graph`, and `name` — because that graph is the function's rebuildable structure. Then, below it, it appends a safe SVG line plot of the function sampled over a finite window of its domain: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static with(Functions) { val fn = sin(10) over (0.0..3.0) fn.h } ``` ![Fn reflective tree with an appended SVG sine plot](assets/value_visualizers/fn_sin_plot.png){ width="612" } The plot mirrors `Fn`'s own sampling rules: an unbounded domain falls back to a preview window, non-finite samples become gaps in the curve rather than spikes, a zero-straddling range draws a dashed baseline, and faint labels mark the value and domain extents (here `1.159 / −1.159` over `0 … 3`). If a function is non-finite everywhere, or its `evalFn` throws, the plot is simply omitted and the tree stands on its own — the value display is never allowed to fail. ### Images, edges, corners and flow The [imaging / computer-vision family](imaging_examples.md) gets the same treatment, and it is the case where the picture most obviously beats the text: an `Img` is a `FloatArray` you cannot read, a `List` is forty records of three doubles each, and a `GaussianPyramid` is `GaussianPyramid@3f1a2b`. Every imaging value below is rendered by `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ImagingVisualizer.kt`, reached through the same `.h` you have been using all along. Evaluate an `Img` and you get the actual pixels, aspect-correct, plus a `
` disclosure holding the per-channel strip, a per-channel histogram computed over the *full-resolution* samples, and the numbers: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(240, 180) { x, y -> /* … */ } scene.h ``` ![An RGB Img with its channel strip, histogram and statistics](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgb.png){ width="564" } #### The range policy This family is **float-channel and unbounded**. A Sobel `dx` is signed. An unnormalised response exceeds 1. An upstream division produces a NaN. A visualizer that just clamps everything to `0…1` answers all three questions with a flat white rectangle. So the renderer picks one of three modes and **always names the one it picked**: `direct` — every finite sample is already in `0…1`. Nothing is rescaled, and the caption says `direct`. That is the picture above. `signed ±m` — some sample is negative. The range is made symmetric about zero, so that *zero is a fixed, recognisable colour* rather than wherever `min…max` happened to put it, and a 1-channel image is run through the `coolwarm` diverging ramp from [`Colormaps`](rectsl_cheatsheet.md) — blue negative, pale zero, red positive. Grey simply cannot carry a sign: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static scene.luma().sobel().dx.h ``` ![A signed Sobel dx rendered with a coolwarm diverging map](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_signed_dx.png){ width="752" } Read it: the rectangle's left edge is red (dark→bright going right, so `dx > 0`) and its right edge is blue; the disc is warm on its left limb and cool on its right. `mean = 0.0002` and `σ = 0.052`, with the histogram spiking at zero, is what a gradient of a mostly-flat image should look like. The disclosure offers the same data read two more ways — plain `grey` and `viridis` — so you get three readings of one response image. `auto-ranged` — non-negative, but the maximum is above 1. Rescaled for display with the **true range printed**, so a bright pixel is never mistaken for 1.0: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static (scene.luma().sobelMagnitude() * 25f).h ``` ![An unnormalised response, auto-ranged with its true 0…10.26 range printed](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_autoranged.png){ width="752" } And non-finite samples — NaN, ±∞ — are counted, excluded from every statistic, and painted **magenta**: ![An image with a NaN block and one infinity, painted magenta](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_non_finite.png){ width="752" } Magenta because the alternative is silence: one NaN poisons `min()`/`max()`, `normalized()` returns an all-NaN image, and the PNG quantiser turns NaN into `0`, so a broken image comes back as an **all-black** thumbnail captioned `range NaN…NaN`. An image that is wrong should look wrong. Four-channel images sit on a checkerboard, so transparent black and opaque black are different pictures: ![An RGBA image over a checkerboard, with its alpha channel broken out](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgba.png){ width="732" } #### Gradients and pyramids A `Gradient` is two signed images and a direction, so it shows all of it — `dx`, `dy`, the magnitude, and the hue-by-direction image the type already knows how to build: ![A Gradient shown as dx, dy, magnitude and hue-by-direction](assets/imaging_visualizers/gradient.png){ width="752" } A pyramid is drawn as a **ladder of rungs at true relative scale**, bottom-aligned, so the halving is the visible fact rather than a number in a caption: ![A GaussianPyramid as five rungs at true relative scale](assets/imaging_visualizers/gaussian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } ![A LaplacianPyramid: signed band rungs plus a tagged residual](assets/imaging_visualizers/laplacian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } The Laplacian bands are signed, so they get the diverging treatment, and the one rung that is *not* a band is labelled `residual`. #### Detector output A `List` becomes a scatter with detector strength as both radius and `viridis` colour. A corner list carries no image extent, so the canvas is the points' own bounding box unioned with the origin — image coordinates start at `(0, 0)`, and including it keeps the points where they actually sit in the frame. The caption states the inferred extent: ![Harris corners as a strength-coded scatter](assets/imaging_visualizers/corners.png){ width="752" } The four strongest here read back as `(30.7, 26.7)`, `(89.3, 26.7)`, `(30.7, 75.3)`, `(89.3, 75.3)` — the four corners of a rectangle planted at `x 30…90, y 26…76` — and the single strongest is where the two rulings cross. A `HoughLine` is `(rho, theta)`: an **infinite** line with no extent of its own, which is why `toFLine` insists on being handed the image dimensions. With no image in reach the left panel clips each line into the smallest square every peak can still cross, says which square that was, and points at `linesToFLines` for the in-place version. The right panel needs no extent at all and is therefore exact: ρ against θ, sized by votes. ![Hough lines in an inferred square, beside their (theta, rho) accumulator peaks](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_lines.png){ width="752" } A circle *does* have an extent, so no assumption is needed: ![Hough circles drawn over their own extent](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_circles.png){ width="752" } A `FlowField` is a quiver — one arrow per converged track, hue by direction, and **failed tracks drawn as grey crosses** rather than dropped. A tracker that never reports failure is lying, and so is a picture that hides the failures. Displacements are drawn at true pixel scale unless the median motion is too small to see, in which case an integer exaggeration factor is applied and named: ![An optical-flow field as a hue-coded quiver, tracing a planted rotation](assets/imaging_visualizers/flow_field.png){ width="752" } The frames here differ by a 0.06 rad rotation about the centre, and that is exactly what the arrows trace: little motion near the middle, tangential motion at the edges, the hue rotating smoothly with the direction. Finally, a `ComponentLabelling` shows the label map under a golden-ratio hue rotation — adjacent label ids get unrelated colours, which is what makes two touching blobs distinguishable at thumbnail size — with the per-blob areas and centroids behind the disclosure: ![A connected-component label map with one hue per blob](assets/imaging_visualizers/components.png){ width="752" } A plain `List` becomes a filmstrip, which is the shape a frame sequence or a parameter sweep already has: ![A List as a filmstrip of a blur sweep](assets/imaging_visualizers/filmstrip.png){ width="752" } #### All of it, in a real box Everything above is a fragment rendered on its own. Here is the same renderer inside an actual Field box, in Field's own output areas: a whole pipeline, with `.h` doing all the work. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-imaging-panels.png" alt="four imaging panels in a row, each a thumbnail over a line of metadata and a row of disclosure links. An RGB image of a yellow rectangle and a cyan disc on a four-way colour gradient, labelled 180x132, rgb, range 0.1 to 0.98; a signed Sobel response of the same scene painted in the blue-white-red coolwarm map, labelled range -0.4083 to 0.4089, signed; a GaussianPyramid as four rungs at true relative scale, 180x132 down to 22x16; and a List of 9 Corners as coloured dots on black, labelled with its response range and an inferred extent of 118.23 by 106.17" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="8" w="1200" h="700" embed=true name="imaging-panels"} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(180, 132) { x, y -> var r = 0.10f + 0.30f * (x / 179f) var g = 0.12f + 0.22f * (y / 131f) var b = 0.34f - 0.20f * (x / 179f) if (x in 24..68 && y in 20..56) { r = 0.94f g = 0.86f b = 0.42f } if (hypot(x - 128.0, y - 46.0) <= 22.0) { r = 0.30f g = 0.80f b = 0.92f } if (x in 112..113 || y in 104..105) { r = 0.98f g = 0.98f b = 0.98f } Triple(r, g, b) } val gray = scene.luma() // Four stages of one pipeline, four different value types, one `.h` each. showRow keeps // them in a single output channel instead of four tall ones. val panels = [ scene.h, // direct mode, 3 channels gray.sobel().dx.h, // signed -> coolwarm diverging gray.gaussianPyramid(4).h, // rungs at true relative scale gray.harrisCorners(minDistance = 6, maxCount = 20).h, // scatter, strength-coded ] showRow("panels", panels) println("imaging visualizers ready") ``` Note what is *not* in that code: no `showImg`, no PNG encoding, no colour-map choice, no normalisation, no per-type branching. `.h` is the whole interface, and the renderer decides per value whether it is looking at colour data, a signed response, a pyramid, or a list of detections. !!! tip "Open the demo document" The [imaging_visualizers_demo](agent_transcripts.md#imaging_visualizers_demo) starting point has one box per visualizer on this page. Open it from the welcome screen, run the boxes and look at each one's output area — every box evaluates one imaging value as its last expression, so there is no `showImg`, no `display(...)` and no explicit call at all. Then change a sigma or a threshold and re-run a box. The rest of this page is the *instruments* built on top of this renderer: inline probes that live next to a line of code, display channels, control surfaces, and synth scopes. ## Inline editor visualizers These draw next to the line of code that produced the value. The core pattern is: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val m = __m("some-marker") m.histogram(0.42) ``` The marker remembers a little state and renders HTML back into the editor gutter / inline output location for that line. ### Histogram, history, and summary stats Histograms answer “what values have I seen?”, history answers “how did the value move?”, and stats gives you a one-line summary. The live examples below are all `loop { }` bodies, which is Field's frame loop: the body runs, then the frame advances, once per Runloop tick. What that tick is, and what stops one of these, is [Frames and the animation loop](animation_time_model.md). ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-metrics.mp4" wait="1.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-metrics"} :::static var tick = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 println("inline metrics ready") loop { tick += 0.4 visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val value = sin(tick * 0.22) * 0.7 + cos(tick * 0.11) * 0.2 + tick * 0.01 __m("histogram").histogram(value, dur = 120) __m("trail").history(value, dur = 48) __m("summary").stats(value, dur = 48) } frame() } ``` Those three calls all share the same basic idea: - `ᛟ.histogram(value)` keeps a rolling distribution. - `ᛟ.history(value)` keeps a rolling time series. - `ᛟ.stats(value)` gives a compact summary panel. In the editor you can add a marker rune (ᛟ), with f1, "Insert Stack Mark", or shift+command period: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin capture="ui" region="window" clip-selector=".afield-palette-shell" screenshot="assets/insert-stack-mark.png" alt="Insert stack mark command" padding="6" wait="0" timeout="90" embed=true hidden=true name="insert-stack-mark"} ui.openEditor(id) ui.pause(700) ui.waitForSelector(".monaco-editor", 15000.0) ui.clickSelector(".monaco-editor") ui.pause(300) ui.press("F1") ui.waitForSelector(".afield-palette-shell", 8000.0) ui.pause(400) ui.type("stack") ui.pause(1200) ``` These functions are **passthroughs**. They return the value they were given, so you can drop them into a chain when you want to inspect the value flowing through a wire without changing the computation: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val filtered = __m("cutoff").history(rawCutoff) ``` That makes them excellent debugging instruments: tiny scopes for values, not transformations of values. If you want a **live** feed rather than a one-shot summary, write a loop and **launch** the box: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-live-history.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-live-history"} :::static println("live history launched") var phase = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val y = sin(phase * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(phase * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) } phase += 0.07 frame() } ``` The same loop is shorter written against the box's `time` instead of a phase it advances itself: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static loop { val t = time val y = sin(t * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(t * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) frame() } ``` Run either as a launch, not a plain execute. ### Piano rolls in the editor The piano-roll visualizer is the same idea, but for scheduled notes rather than scalar values. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-pianoroll.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-pianoroll"} :::static val arp = noteProcess { val chord = [48, 55, 60, 64] var step = 0 while (true) { note( pitch = chord[step % chord.size], duration = 0.18, velocity = 0.85, label = "n$step", ) rest(0.25) step++ } } println("inline piano roll launched") var playhead = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { __m("arp").pianoRoll(arp.at(playhead)) } playhead += 0.35 frame() } ``` Use it for sequencers, generative rhythm systems, or anything where you want to see future note structure without leaving the code. ## Display channels: the big canvas under the box Inline visuals sit beside one line of code. `display(...)` has the whole area under the box. Anything you pass to `display("channel", thing)` becomes HTML in a named output area. That HTML can be handwritten, auto-generated, interactive, or even an embedded browser/inspector. ### Raw HTML, pretty HTML, and heavy HTML - `display("channel", "
...
")` is the raw escape hatch. - `.h` turns a value into a lightweight pretty HTML view. - `.h2` turns a heavier structure into a paged browser / explorer. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-display-html.png" alt="three output channels stacked in one box. 'hello' holds a small blue-bordered card reading 'display(...) can show any HTML you like.'; 'pretty' holds a syntax-coloured dump of a four-entry map with tempo 122, mode mixolydian, active true and notes [C, E, G, Bb]; 'heavy' holds a LinkedHashMap of 18 rows rendered as a scrollable two-column table of key against value, its rows named row-0 upward and every value a Map of size 10" wait="4.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" embed=true name="display-html"} :::static val tiny = linkedMapOf( "tempo" to 122, "mode" to "mixolydian", "active" to true, "notes" to ["C", "E", "G", "Bb"], ) val big = (0 until 18).associate { row -> "row-$row" to (0 until 10).associate { col -> "c$col" to row * col } } display( "hello", "
" + "display(...) can show any HTML you like." + "
", ) display("pretty", tiny.h) display("heavy", big.h2) println("display helpers ready") ``` Use `.h` when the structure is small enough that you want a pleasant, immediate rendering. Use `.h2` when you want to browse instead of read. That covers a large map, list, array or buffer without turning the output area into soup, and it covers your own data classes and Field's own types too. `.h2` on a plain object gives you its properties as a scrollable table: one row per property, with its declared type and its value. Above the table sit `outliner` and `columns` links, which open the same value in the full tree and column browsers. There is nothing to register; it reflects. If a property's getter throws, the row is still there, marked, with the exception text in its value cell. Four things are special-cased, because their fields are not where the interesting content is. A `Box` shows its name, frame, code size, run state, its whole property bag, and a table of its `parents`, `children`, `nested` and `nestedIn` edges. An `Fn` shows a sampled table of `x` and `f(x)` across its domain, because a function is its values and its one substantive field is a private closure. An `FLine` shows its node table: instruction kind, control-point count and endpoint per row. An exception shows its message, its cause chain and its stack. Some values `.h2` hands straight back to `.h`, because the compact rendering already *is* the value: numbers, strings, enums, a `Pair`, a vector, a matrix (which `.h` draws as a heatmap), and a `Quantity`, whose whole point is a number next to a unit. To see all of it at once, insert the **h2 Explorer Examples** template and run its boxes top to bottom. ### Markdown for captions and tables The escape hatch above has a way of taking over. A figure that wants a heading, a key/value table and a block of computed text ends up as a hundred lines of string concatenation, with a hand-picked font stack, a `` builder and a local `fun esc(s: String)`, often longer than the code it illustrates. `markdown("channel", "…")` says the same thing in markdown, and picks up Field's own `--field-*` tokens instead of re-inventing them: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-markdown.png" alt="one markdown card headed 'what the run settled on'. A two-column reading/value table gives tempo 122, drift -0.004 and voice 'saw 110 *'. Under it a status line reads stable, budget 83% used in amber, no retries. Then a two-column row labelled BEFORE and AFTER, holding gain 0.2 on the left and gain 0.9 on the right, and a quoted solver-output block reading 'converged in 41 steps, residual 3.2e-7'" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" embed=true name="display-markdown"} :::static val readings = linkedMapOf("tempo" to 122, "drift" to -0.004, "voice" to "saw 110 *") val rows = readings.entries.joinToString("\n") { (k, v) -> "| ${k.md} | ${v.md} |" } val report = "converged in 41 steps\nresidual 3.2e-7" markdown( "figure", """ ### what the run settled on | reading | value | |---------|-------| $rows status: {ok:**stable**} · budget: {warn:83% used} · {muted:no retries} :::row #### before ${mapOf("gain" to 0.2).h} --- #### after ${mapOf("gain" to 0.9).h} :::end #### solver output ~~~ $report ~~~ """, width = 820, ) println("markdown figure ready") ``` Three rules matter once a figure mixes computed values into the prose: - **HTML passes through, inline and block.** `.h`, `diffHtml()`, `graphSvg()` and friends already return HTML; interpolate them directly and they land verbatim, table cells included. Only text you actually wrote as markdown gets escaped. - **`value.md` for computed values.** Runtime values are not markdown — a `|` splits the row it lands in, a pair of `*` becomes emphasis, a `` is read as a tag and vanishes. Escape anything you did not write yourself. `mdEscape(value)` is the same function, written as a call. - **Fenced bodies are interpolated at column zero**, hard left, the way `$report` is above. Inside a fence whitespace is the content, and splicing at the surrounding indentation would indent only the value's first line. Beyond GitHub-flavoured markdown there are two additions: `:::row … :::end`, splitting columns on a `---` line, for the before/after shape markdown cannot spell; and `{role:text}` spans — `accent`, `muted`, `dim`, `ok`, `warn`, `bad` — so a callout never needs a hex literal. Neither applies inside code, so a `:::row` or a `{warn:…}` shown *as* an example stays as written. The figure above uses both: the before/after row, and the `ok`, `warn` and `muted` spans on its status line. You do not need `trimIndent()`; the text is dedented for you, and unlike `trimIndent` it survives having a multi-line value interpolated into it. `width` pins the card's width; without it the card is as wide as its widest unbreakable line. ### Trees and columns For a value you want to browse like a little filesystem, open it in a tree or column browser. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-display-browsers.png" alt="two inspector channels over the same nested scene map. 'outline' is a tree browser with camera expanded to show x, y, zoom and active, and layers and palette still folded. A plain drag works like `vec2Control(...)`, and the callback gets each position. **Shift-drag** records a take: the whole stroke and its timing, kept with the box like any other control value. On a phone, tap **rec**, then draw. The trail of the take stays on the pad. The box replays the take, and the box keeps the time. `at(seconds)` returns where the take is that far into its loop, interpolated between the recorded samples, and `playhead(seconds)` puts a ring on the pad there. Read both off the clock in a `loop`, as the sequencer does, and the replay never drifts and keeps going with the browser closed. `initialTake` gives the pad something to play before you have recorded anything; here it is a figure eight: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-gesture.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="4" fps="20" timeout="180" w="600" embed=true name="gesture" alt="an XY pad headed MOVE with the readout 2.0 s take and a rec button. Use it for anything with two axes: a camera, a pan and a filter, a point in a preset space. To edit a take key by key, bake it into keyframe lanes with `bakeGesture(pad)`, and send the edited lanes back with `pad.setTake(x, y)`: see [From a performed gesture](keyframe_editor.md#from-a-performed-gesture). ### Choosing the right control - Use `slider(...)` for one bounded numeric value. - Use `vec2Control(...)` for direction, position, velocity, or any paired numeric parameter. - Use `checkbox(...)` for feature toggles and gates. - Use `stringInput(...)` for names, labels, prompts, and small text parameters. - Use `colorPicker(...)` for RGBA values stored as normalized `Vector4f` data. - Use `multiSlider(...)` for a row of values you want to draw rather than set one at a time: steps, envelopes, partials. - Use `matrix(...)` for patterns: on/off steps, or several states per cell with `states = n`. - Use `rangeSlider(...)` for an interval, such as a band, a window or a velocity range. Use `polar = true` when the value wraps around, like a phase or a hue. - Use `menu(...)` for choosing one of a few named options. - Use `gesture(...)` for a two-axis movement you want to perform once and loop. - For a curve over time you shape by hand, an envelope, use the keyframe editor, `keyframes(...)`: see [Keyframes and timelines](funFeatures.md#keyframes-and-timelines). The `vec2Control(...)` includes an XY pad, a vector line, and magnitude readout, so it works well for motion and layout values where two sliders would hide the relationship between axes. ## Recorded audio: waveform, player, playhead, and navigation `AudioVisualizer` is the general-purpose recorded-sound view. It combines a waveform and native browser audio controls, keeps an optional vertical playhead synchronized with playback, and uses the waveform itself as a navigator: - click to seek; - drag to pan; - use the mouse wheel or `+` / `−` to zoom while keeping the visible playhead fixed on screen; - shift-wheel to pan; - double-click or press **all** to restore the complete clip. If the playhead is outside the visible interval, wheel zoom falls back to the pointer and button or keyboard zoom falls back to the center. Near the start or end of a recording, boundary clamping may move the playhead on screen. A completion-style spinner remains over the waveform while a newly zoomed or panned min/max envelope is loading, so the old waveform cannot be mistaken for the new view. During playback, crossing the right edge advances the visible interval and places the playhead slightly inside the new window; crossing the left edge after a backward seek mirrors that behavior. Set `followPlayhead = false` in `AudioVisualizerOptions` to keep a zoomed interval stationary. Waveform-envelope requests have a 15-second browser deadline; a stalled service clears the spinner and reports a timeout instead of leaving the view permanently busy. Any subsequent pan, zoom, or resize retries normally. Short sample arrays can be embedded in the page. The visualization endpoint caps previews at 4096 points; zoom and pan never turn the full activation tensor into a large JSON response. Per-job progress can replace a named output with `fieldAudioJobStatusHtml(accepted, event)`, while `fieldAudioJobMonitor()` embeds the complete durable queue. Audio playback moves a marker through both portraits; hovering either portrait publishes the nearest frame time; clicking seeks the player. 'audio' pairs a dense stereo waveform at peak 0.858, rms 0.382 with a spectrum whose harmonics march up to a broad shelf past 5 kHz. 'scope' shows the same pair after filtering: a smaller waveform at peak 0.355 and a spectrum whose partials die away by 5 kHz. 'env' draws an ADSR, the orange gate dropping partway across and the blue level decaying after it, tagged RELEASE, lvl 0.401. So the choice is mostly about **where you want the visual to live**. ## Choosing between inline and display Here is the practical rule of thumb: - If the visual explains one line of code, put it inline on a stack mark (ᛟ, **Insert Stack Mark**). - If the visual explains a whole box or deserves interaction, put it in `display(...)`. - If the thing is large and structural, use `tree(...)`, `column(...)`, or `.h2`. - If the thing is tiny and human-readable, `.h` is often perfect. `histogram(...)` and `history(...)` return the value they were given, so you can leave them in a computation while you debug it. All of these tools compose. One box can have a little inline history, a piano roll, a browser in one output channel, and a control surface in another. Field is very happy when code is also an interface.

# Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments *Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`ValueVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt), [`ImagingVisualizer.kt`](reference/visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt), [`plotly.kt`](reference/visualization.md#plotly-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).* Field has many ways to show a value, and the quickest takes two keystrokes: put `.h` on the end of an expression and run the line. What comes back can land in several places. Some visuals appear **inline in the editor**, beside the line you ran. Some fill an **output area** under the box. Some output areas become **inspectors**, or **little control panels** whose sliders you drag while the code around them keeps running. And helpers like `.h` and `.h2` are about turning an arbitrary Kotlin value into something formatted well enough to read. This page is a tour of the whole family. ## The value visualizer: what `.h` draws Most environments answer "what is this value?" with a line of `toString()`. Field answers with a *picture*: whenever you ask Field to show a value, the **value visualizer** turns it into a compact HTML view — a reflective tree for arbitrary objects, and, for the types Field draws with, a little inline graphic. You reach it three ways, all of which call the same renderer (`ValueVisualizer.visualize(...)`, in `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ValueVisualizer.kt`): ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static value.h // the .h extension: value -> pretty HTML display("inspect", value.h) // drop that HTML into a named output channel box.viz(value = value) // convenience: visualize into the box's "viz" channel ``` `.h` is the lightweight view used throughout Field; its heavier sibling `.h2` opens a paged browser for large structures. The built-in and reflective paths are forgiving: they track recursion by reference, cap depth and preview sizes, catch reflective getter failures, and guard optional plots and thumbnails (including a throwing `Fn.evalFn`). Objects implementing `ToHTML` and callbacks registered with `registerValuePrinter` are extension points whose returned HTML is trusted. `registerValuePrinter` is how a **third-party** type joins in without knowing Field exists, and the worked example is a Kotlin DataFrame: a frame, a column, a row and a `GroupBy` all render as ordinary Field tables, and `.h2` pages a million-row frame through the same offset machinery this page's `.h2` uses everywhere else. See [DataFrames in a Box](dataframe.md#looking-at-a-frame). ### The reflective tree Give the visualizer an ordinary object — a data class, a map, anything with readable properties — and it walks the members into an indented tree. Numbers, booleans, strings, and nested values are each rendered by the same rules, recursively. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static data class Camera( val position: Vector3f, val fieldOfView: Double, val active: Boolean, val layers: List, ) val cam = Camera(Vector3f(0f, 1.5f, -4f), 55.0, true, ["dots", "lines", "labels"]) cam.h ``` ![Reflective tree for a Camera data class](assets/value_visualizers/reflective_tree.png){ width="516" } Notice that the tree is not flat text: the nested `position` is itself rendered as a `vec3`, and `layers` collapses to a list with a size count. The renderer keeps only a handful of fields inline (with a "… +N more fields" expander for the rest) so a large object never floods the output. ### Numeric collections, with stats Arrays and lists of numbers get a preview plus a one-line statistical summary — mean, standard deviation, and range — so you can judge a buffer without scrolling through it. Long collections elide the middle: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val samples = DoubleArray(48) { i -> sin(i / 48.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI) } samples.h ``` ![DoubleArray preview with mean, sigma and range](assets/value_visualizers/double_array.png) The tail reads `… +28 more items [μ=8.90e-17, σ=0.707, range=−1…1] (48)`: the sampled sine averages to ~0, has the expected 0.707 RMS spread, and spans −1…1 — visible immediately, without a plot. The same treatment applies to `IntArray`, `FloatArray`, and numeric `List`s. ### Vectors, matrices, and quaternions Field's generated linear-algebra types render as compact, colour-coded tokens rather than as reflective trees — the point of a `vec3` is its three numbers, not its class internals: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static [vec(0.5, 1.5), vec(1.0, 2.0, 3.0), vec(0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0)].h ``` ![vec2, vec3 and vec4 rendered as compact tokens](assets/value_visualizers/vectors.png){ width="324" } Matrices summarise rather than dump every cell: a `mat3` shows its determinant, a `mat4` shows determinant plus extracted translation, and a quaternion shows its four components. Here they are keyed by a map, which the visualizer renders as a tree — a good way to label several related values at once: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static linkedMapOf( "scale (mat3)" to Matrix3f().set(2f, 0f, 0f, 0f, 3f, 0f, 0f, 0f, 1f), "translate (mat4)" to Matrix4f().identity().apply { set(3, 0, 5f) set(3, 1, -2f) set(3, 2, 1f) }, "spin (quat)" to Quaternionf().rotateY(0.6f), ) .h ``` ![A map of mat3, mat4 and quaternion values](assets/value_visualizers/linalg_map.png){ width="564" } The `mat3` reports `det=6` (2 × 3 × 1), the `mat4` reports `det=1, t=(5, -2, 1)`, and the quaternion shows its normalized components. For the algebra behind these types, see [Linear Algebra](linear_algebra.md). ### An `FLine`, drawn An [`FLine`](fline_examples.md) — Field's core drawable path — is where the renderer stops summarising and starts *drawing*. Alongside its node counts, bounding box, length, and a compressed path signature, it appends a small inline SVG thumbnail of the actual geometry: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val spiral = FLine() val steps = 140 spiral.breakNext() for (i in 0..steps) { val t = i.toDouble() / steps val a = t * 5.0 * 2.0 * Math.PI val r = 8.0 + t * 60.0 val x = 80.0 + Math.cos(a) * r val y = 80.0 + Math.sin(a) * r spiral.lineTo(x, y) } spiral.h ``` ![FLine node stats, path signature, and an SVG spiral thumbnail](assets/value_visualizers/fline_spiral.png){ width="552" } The header reads `FLine (141 nodes)`, then `M=1 L=140 C=0 · b=130×124 · len=1.19e+03`, then the run-compressed signature `M(Lx41) … (Lx22)`, and finally the thumbnail. The thumbnail is normalised into its box and only rendered for paths under a complexity budget, so pasting a huge path into a value view never becomes a rendering hazard. ### An `Fn`, plotted The richest case is a [`Functions.Fn`](functions_examples.md). Field keeps the full reflective tree — its `domain`, `evalFn`, `graph`, and `name` — because that graph is the function's rebuildable structure. Then, below it, it appends a safe SVG line plot of the function sampled over a finite window of its domain: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static with(Functions) { val fn = sin(10) over (0.0..3.0) fn.h } ``` ![Fn reflective tree with an appended SVG sine plot](assets/value_visualizers/fn_sin_plot.png){ width="612" } The plot mirrors `Fn`'s own sampling rules: an unbounded domain falls back to a preview window, non-finite samples become gaps in the curve rather than spikes, a zero-straddling range draws a dashed baseline, and faint labels mark the value and domain extents (here `1.159 / −1.159` over `0 … 3`). If a function is non-finite everywhere, or its `evalFn` throws, the plot is simply omitted and the tree stands on its own — the value display is never allowed to fail. ### Images, edges, corners and flow The [imaging / computer-vision family](imaging_examples.md) gets the same treatment, and it is the case where the picture most obviously beats the text: an `Img` is a `FloatArray` you cannot read, a `List` is forty records of three doubles each, and a `GaussianPyramid` is `GaussianPyramid@3f1a2b`. Every imaging value below is rendered by `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ImagingVisualizer.kt`, reached through the same `.h` you have been using all along. Evaluate an `Img` and you get the actual pixels, aspect-correct, plus a `
` disclosure holding the per-channel strip, a per-channel histogram computed over the *full-resolution* samples, and the numbers: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(240, 180) { x, y -> /* … */ } scene.h ``` ![An RGB Img with its channel strip, histogram and statistics](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgb.png){ width="564" } #### The range policy This family is **float-channel and unbounded**. A Sobel `dx` is signed. An unnormalised response exceeds 1. An upstream division produces a NaN. A visualizer that just clamps everything to `0…1` answers all three questions with a flat white rectangle. So the renderer picks one of three modes and **always names the one it picked**: `direct` — every finite sample is already in `0…1`. Nothing is rescaled, and the caption says `direct`. That is the picture above. `signed ±m` — some sample is negative. The range is made symmetric about zero, so that *zero is a fixed, recognisable colour* rather than wherever `min…max` happened to put it, and a 1-channel image is run through the `coolwarm` diverging ramp from [`Colormaps`](rectsl_cheatsheet.md) — blue negative, pale zero, red positive. Grey simply cannot carry a sign: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static scene.luma().sobel().dx.h ``` ![A signed Sobel dx rendered with a coolwarm diverging map](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_signed_dx.png){ width="752" } Read it: the rectangle's left edge is red (dark→bright going right, so `dx > 0`) and its right edge is blue; the disc is warm on its left limb and cool on its right. `mean = 0.0002` and `σ = 0.052`, with the histogram spiking at zero, is what a gradient of a mostly-flat image should look like. The disclosure offers the same data read two more ways — plain `grey` and `viridis` — so you get three readings of one response image. `auto-ranged` — non-negative, but the maximum is above 1. Rescaled for display with the **true range printed**, so a bright pixel is never mistaken for 1.0: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static (scene.luma().sobelMagnitude() * 25f).h ``` ![An unnormalised response, auto-ranged with its true 0…10.26 range printed](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_autoranged.png){ width="752" } And non-finite samples — NaN, ±∞ — are counted, excluded from every statistic, and painted **magenta**: ![An image with a NaN block and one infinity, painted magenta](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_non_finite.png){ width="752" } Magenta because the alternative is silence: one NaN poisons `min()`/`max()`, `normalized()` returns an all-NaN image, and the PNG quantiser turns NaN into `0`, so a broken image comes back as an **all-black** thumbnail captioned `range NaN…NaN`. An image that is wrong should look wrong. Four-channel images sit on a checkerboard, so transparent black and opaque black are different pictures: ![An RGBA image over a checkerboard, with its alpha channel broken out](assets/imaging_visualizers/img_rgba.png){ width="732" } #### Gradients and pyramids A `Gradient` is two signed images and a direction, so it shows all of it — `dx`, `dy`, the magnitude, and the hue-by-direction image the type already knows how to build: ![A Gradient shown as dx, dy, magnitude and hue-by-direction](assets/imaging_visualizers/gradient.png){ width="752" } A pyramid is drawn as a **ladder of rungs at true relative scale**, bottom-aligned, so the halving is the visible fact rather than a number in a caption: ![A GaussianPyramid as five rungs at true relative scale](assets/imaging_visualizers/gaussian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } ![A LaplacianPyramid: signed band rungs plus a tagged residual](assets/imaging_visualizers/laplacian_pyramid.png){ width="752" } The Laplacian bands are signed, so they get the diverging treatment, and the one rung that is *not* a band is labelled `residual`. #### Detector output A `List` becomes a scatter with detector strength as both radius and `viridis` colour. A corner list carries no image extent, so the canvas is the points' own bounding box unioned with the origin — image coordinates start at `(0, 0)`, and including it keeps the points where they actually sit in the frame. The caption states the inferred extent: ![Harris corners as a strength-coded scatter](assets/imaging_visualizers/corners.png){ width="752" } The four strongest here read back as `(30.7, 26.7)`, `(89.3, 26.7)`, `(30.7, 75.3)`, `(89.3, 75.3)` — the four corners of a rectangle planted at `x 30…90, y 26…76` — and the single strongest is where the two rulings cross. A `HoughLine` is `(rho, theta)`: an **infinite** line with no extent of its own, which is why `toFLine` insists on being handed the image dimensions. With no image in reach the left panel clips each line into the smallest square every peak can still cross, says which square that was, and points at `linesToFLines` for the in-place version. The right panel needs no extent at all and is therefore exact: ρ against θ, sized by votes. ![Hough lines in an inferred square, beside their (theta, rho) accumulator peaks](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_lines.png){ width="752" } A circle *does* have an extent, so no assumption is needed: ![Hough circles drawn over their own extent](assets/imaging_visualizers/hough_circles.png){ width="752" } A `FlowField` is a quiver — one arrow per converged track, hue by direction, and **failed tracks drawn as grey crosses** rather than dropped. A tracker that never reports failure is lying, and so is a picture that hides the failures. Displacements are drawn at true pixel scale unless the median motion is too small to see, in which case an integer exaggeration factor is applied and named: ![An optical-flow field as a hue-coded quiver, tracing a planted rotation](assets/imaging_visualizers/flow_field.png){ width="752" } The frames here differ by a 0.06 rad rotation about the centre, and that is exactly what the arrows trace: little motion near the middle, tangential motion at the edges, the hue rotating smoothly with the direction. Finally, a `ComponentLabelling` shows the label map under a golden-ratio hue rotation — adjacent label ids get unrelated colours, which is what makes two touching blobs distinguishable at thumbnail size — with the per-blob areas and centroids behind the disclosure: ![A connected-component label map with one hue per blob](assets/imaging_visualizers/components.png){ width="752" } A plain `List` becomes a filmstrip, which is the shape a frame sequence or a parameter sweep already has: ![A List as a filmstrip of a blur sweep](assets/imaging_visualizers/filmstrip.png){ width="752" } #### All of it, in a real box Everything above is a fragment rendered on its own. Here is the same renderer inside an actual Field box, in Field's own output areas: a whole pipeline, with `.h` doing all the work. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-imaging-panels.png" alt="four imaging panels in a row, each a thumbnail over a line of metadata and a row of disclosure links. An RGB image of a yellow rectangle and a cyan disc on a four-way colour gradient, labelled 180x132, rgb, range 0.1 to 0.98; a signed Sobel response of the same scene painted in the blue-white-red coolwarm map, labelled range -0.4083 to 0.4089, signed; a GaussianPyramid as four rungs at true relative scale, 180x132 down to 22x16; and a List of 9 Corners as coloured dots on black, labelled with its response range and an inferred extent of 118.23 by 106.17" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="8" w="1200" h="700" embed=true name="imaging-panels"} :::static val scene = Img.generateRGB(180, 132) { x, y -> var r = 0.10f + 0.30f * (x / 179f) var g = 0.12f + 0.22f * (y / 131f) var b = 0.34f - 0.20f * (x / 179f) if (x in 24..68 && y in 20..56) { r = 0.94f g = 0.86f b = 0.42f } if (hypot(x - 128.0, y - 46.0) <= 22.0) { r = 0.30f g = 0.80f b = 0.92f } if (x in 112..113 || y in 104..105) { r = 0.98f g = 0.98f b = 0.98f } Triple(r, g, b) } val gray = scene.luma() // Four stages of one pipeline, four different value types, one `.h` each. showRow keeps // them in a single output channel instead of four tall ones. val panels = [ scene.h, // direct mode, 3 channels gray.sobel().dx.h, // signed -> coolwarm diverging gray.gaussianPyramid(4).h, // rungs at true relative scale gray.harrisCorners(minDistance = 6, maxCount = 20).h, // scatter, strength-coded ] showRow("panels", panels) println("imaging visualizers ready") ``` Note what is *not* in that code: no `showImg`, no PNG encoding, no colour-map choice, no normalisation, no per-type branching. `.h` is the whole interface, and the renderer decides per value whether it is looking at colour data, a signed response, a pyramid, or a list of detections. !!! tip "Open the demo document" The [imaging_visualizers_demo](agent_transcripts.md#imaging_visualizers_demo) starting point has one box per visualizer on this page. Open it from the welcome screen, run the boxes and look at each one's output area — every box evaluates one imaging value as its last expression, so there is no `showImg`, no `display(...)` and no explicit call at all. Then change a sigma or a threshold and re-run a box. The rest of this page is the *instruments* built on top of this renderer: inline probes that live next to a line of code, display channels, control surfaces, and synth scopes. ## Inline editor visualizers These draw next to the line of code that produced the value. The core pattern is: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val m = __m("some-marker") m.histogram(0.42) ``` The marker remembers a little state and renders HTML back into the editor gutter / inline output location for that line. ### Histogram, history, and summary stats Histograms answer “what values have I seen?”, history answers “how did the value move?”, and stats gives you a one-line summary. The live examples below are all `loop { }` bodies, which is Field's frame loop: the body runs, then the frame advances, once per Runloop tick. What that tick is, and what stops one of these, is [Frames and the animation loop](animation_time_model.md). ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-metrics.mp4" wait="1.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-metrics"} :::static var tick = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 println("inline metrics ready") loop { tick += 0.4 visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val value = sin(tick * 0.22) * 0.7 + cos(tick * 0.11) * 0.2 + tick * 0.01 __m("histogram").histogram(value, dur = 120) __m("trail").history(value, dur = 48) __m("summary").stats(value, dur = 48) } frame() } ``` Those three calls all share the same basic idea: - `ᛟ.histogram(value)` keeps a rolling distribution. - `ᛟ.history(value)` keeps a rolling time series. - `ᛟ.stats(value)` gives a compact summary panel. In the editor you can add a marker rune (ᛟ), with f1, "Insert Stack Mark", or shift+command period: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin capture="ui" region="window" clip-selector=".afield-palette-shell" screenshot="assets/insert-stack-mark.png" alt="Insert stack mark command" padding="6" wait="0" timeout="90" embed=true hidden=true name="insert-stack-mark"} ui.openEditor(id) ui.pause(700) ui.waitForSelector(".monaco-editor", 15000.0) ui.clickSelector(".monaco-editor") ui.pause(300) ui.press("F1") ui.waitForSelector(".afield-palette-shell", 8000.0) ui.pause(400) ui.type("stack") ui.pause(1200) ``` These functions are **passthroughs**. They return the value they were given, so you can drop them into a chain when you want to inspect the value flowing through a wire without changing the computation: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val filtered = __m("cutoff").history(rawCutoff) ``` That makes them excellent debugging instruments: tiny scopes for values, not transformations of values. If you want a **live** feed rather than a one-shot summary, write a loop and **launch** the box: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-live-history.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-live-history"} :::static println("live history launched") var phase = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { val y = sin(phase * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(phase * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) } phase += 0.07 frame() } ``` The same loop is shorter written against the box's `time` instead of a phase it advances itself: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static loop { val t = time val y = sin(t * 0.8) + 0.2 * sin(t * 7.0) __m("live").history(y, dur = 120) frame() } ``` Run either as a launch, not a plain execute. ### Piano rolls in the editor The piano-roll visualizer is the same idea, but for scheduled notes rather than scalar values. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-inline-pianoroll.mp4" wait="2.0" capture="editor" outputs="inline" padding="10" execution="launch" duration="3" fps="12" timeout="120" embed=true name="inline-pianoroll"} :::static val arp = noteProcess { val chord = [48, 55, 60, 64] var step = 0 while (true) { note( pitch = chord[step % chord.size], duration = 0.18, velocity = 0.85, label = "n$step", ) rest(0.25) step++ } } println("inline piano roll launched") var playhead = 0.0 var visualizerFrame = 0 loop { visualizerFrame += 1 if (visualizerFrame % 2 == 0) { __m("arp").pianoRoll(arp.at(playhead)) } playhead += 0.35 frame() } ``` Use it for sequencers, generative rhythm systems, or anything where you want to see future note structure without leaving the code. ## Display channels: the big canvas under the box Inline visuals sit beside one line of code. `display(...)` has the whole area under the box. Anything you pass to `display("channel", thing)` becomes HTML in a named output area. That HTML can be handwritten, auto-generated, interactive, or even an embedded browser/inspector. ### Raw HTML, pretty HTML, and heavy HTML - `display("channel", "
...

Use `.h2` when you want to browse instead of read. That covers a large map, list, array or buffer without turning the output area into soup, and it covers your own data classes and Field's own types too. `.h2` on a plain object gives you its properties as a scrollable table: one row per property, with its declared type and its value. Above the table sit `outliner` and `columns` links, which open the same value in the full tree and column browsers. There is nothing to register; it reflects. If a property's getter throws, the row is still there, marked, with the exception text in its value cell. Four things are special-cased, because their fields are not where the interesting content is. A `Box` shows its name, frame, code size, run state, its whole property bag, and a table of its `parents`, `children`, `nested` and `nestedIn` edges. An `Fn` shows a sampled table of `x` and `f(x)` across its domain, because a function is its values and its one substantive field is a private closure. An `FLine` shows its node table: instruction kind, control-point count and endpoint per row. An exception shows its message, its cause chain and its stack. Some values `.h2` hands straight back to `.h`, because the compact rendering already *is* the value: numbers, strings, enums, a `Pair`, a vector, a matrix (which `.h` draws as a heatmap), and a `Quantity`, whose whole point is a number next to a unit. To see all of it at once, insert the **h2 Explorer Examples** template and run its boxes top to bottom. ### Markdown for captions and tables The escape hatch above has a way of taking over. A figure that wants a heading, a key/value table and a block of computed text ends up as a hundred lines of string concatenation, with a hand-picked font stack, a `` builder and a local `fun esc(s: String)`, often longer than the code it illustrates. `markdown("channel", "…")` says the same thing in markdown, and picks up Field's own `--field-*` tokens instead of re-inventing them: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-markdown.png" alt="one markdown card headed 'what the run settled on'. A two-column reading/value table gives tempo 122, drift -0.004 and voice 'saw 110 *'. Under it a status line reads stable, budget 83% used in amber, no retries. Then a two-column row labelled BEFORE and AFTER, holding gain 0.2 on the left and gain 0.9 on the right, and a quoted solver-output block reading 'converged in 41 steps, residual 3.2e-7'" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="900" embed=true name="display-markdown"} :::static val readings = linkedMapOf("tempo" to 122, "drift" to -0.004, "voice" to "saw 110 *") val rows = readings.entries.joinToString("\n") { (k, v) -> "| ${k.md} | ${v.md} |" } val report = "converged in 41 steps\nresidual 3.2e-7" markdown( "figure", """ ### what the run settled on | reading | value | |---------|-------| $rows status: {ok:**stable**} · budget: {warn:83% used} · {muted:no retries} :::row #### before ${mapOf("gain" to 0.2).h} --- #### after ${mapOf("gain" to 0.9).h} :::end #### solver output ~~~ $report ~~~ """, width = 820, ) println("markdown figure ready") ``` Three rules matter once a figure mixes computed values into the prose: - **HTML passes through, inline and block.** `.h`, `diffHtml()`, `graphSvg()` and friends already return HTML; interpolate them directly and they land verbatim, table cells included. Only text you actually wrote as markdown gets escaped. - **`value.md` for computed values.** Runtime values are not markdown — a `|` splits the row it lands in, a pair of `*` becomes emphasis, a `` is read as a tag and vanishes. Escape anything you did not write yourself. `mdEscape(value)` is the same function, written as a call. - **Fenced bodies are interpolated at column zero**, hard left, the way `$report` is above. Inside a fence whitespace is the content, and splicing at the surrounding indentation would indent only the value's first line. Beyond GitHub-flavoured markdown there are two additions: `:::row … :::end`, splitting columns on a `---` line, for the before/after shape markdown cannot spell; and `{role:text}` spans — `accent`, `muted`, `dim`, `ok`, `warn`, `bad` — so a callout never needs a hex literal. Neither applies inside code, so a `:::row` or a `{warn:…}` shown *as* an example stays as written. The figure above uses both: the before/after row, and the `ok`, `warn` and `muted` spans on its status line. You do not need `trimIndent()`; the text is dedented for you, and unlike `trimIndent` it survives having a multi-line value interpolated into it. `width` pins the card's width; without it the card is as wide as its widest unbreakable line. ### Trees and columns For a value you want to browse like a little filesystem, open it in a tree or column browser. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-display-browsers.png" alt="two inspector channels over the same nested scene map. 'outline' is a tree browser with camera expanded to show x, y, zoom and active, and layers and palette still folded. 'columns' is a column browser, its root column listing camera, layers and palette with a scrollbar down the right of the pane" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" h="260" embed=true name="display-browsers"} :::static val scene = linkedMapOf( "camera" to linkedMapOf( "x" to 10, "y" to 20, "zoom" to 1.5, "active" to true, ), "layers" to [ linkedMapOf( "name" to "dots", "visible" to true, "points" to [2, 4, 8, 16], ), linkedMapOf( "name" to "lines", "visible" to false, "style" to linkedMapOf("width" to 2, "color" to "#f2aa4c"), ), ], "palette" to linkedMapOf( "background" to "#101820", "accent" to "#f2aa4c", ), ) tree("outline", scene) column("columns", scene) println("inspector panes ready") ``` - `tree("channel", value)` gives you an outline / tree browser. - `column("channel", value)` gives you a column-style browser. These are especially good for nested maps, scene graphs, structured JSON-like data, or anything you want to poke around in rather than summarize. Both take any value, not only maps and lists. A data class or one of your own classes opens to its public properties, an `IntArray` or `DoubleArray` opens to its elements, and a map whose keys are objects opens each entry to its key and its value. Every row shows its name, its type and a one-line summary (`5000 items`, `"label"`, `Point(x=1.0, y=2.5, label=p)`), so you can read most of a structure without opening anything: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/visualizers-tree-values.png" alt="A tree embed titled LinkedHashMap, 4 entries, with a filter box. Open rows follow the value: if code that keeps running (a `frames { }` loop, say) adds to `particles`, the tree shows the new size within about a second, without re-running the box. An object that contains itself is marked with `↺` instead of being opened forever. Keys, once you have clicked into the embed: the arrow keys move and open (in `column`, `←` and `→` move between columns), `/` filters the rows, `c` copies the selected value as text, `p` copies the row's path, and `r` reloads. The header stays put while the rows scroll. The embed grows with its content up to a height and then scrolls; pass `maxHeight = 800` to `tree` or `column` to change that height. The rows are the same edges [`graphPaths`](graph_query.md) walks, so every row has a path from the value you passed in, such as `particle/position` or `many/250`. Press `p` (or the **path** button on a row) and paste it into box code: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} :::static val age = scene.graphPath("particle/age")?.get() ``` Type a pattern containing `/`, `*` or `|` into the filter and it runs `graphPaths` on the whole value instead of filtering one level: `**/tag` lists every `tag` at any depth, labelled by path. Choose one (Enter, or double-click) and the tree or columns open to it. Plain text still just filters the rows in view. This recording types `**/name` into the filter of a tree over a small scene of groups and layers. Pass `includePrivate = true` to `tree` or `column` to list them; their paths then need `graphPaths(pattern, GraphWalkOptions(includePrivate = true))`. A row has no path when nothing reaches it by name: an element of a primitive array, a map key that is an object, the second of two map keys that print alike. And while it is not a “visualizer” in the chart sense, `logs(...)` belongs in the same family. A plain drag works like `vec2Control(...)`, and the callback gets each position. **Shift-drag** records a take: the whole stroke and its timing, kept with the box like any other control value. On a phone, tap **rec**, then draw. The trail of the take stays on the pad. The box replays the take, and the box keeps the time. `at(seconds)` returns where the take is that far into its loop, interpolated between the recorded samples, and `playhead(seconds)` puts a ring on the pad there. Read both off the clock in a `loop`, as the sequencer does, and the replay never drifts and keeps going with the browser closed. `initialTake` gives the pad something to play before you have recorded anything; here it is a figure eight: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/visualizers-gesture.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="4" fps="20" timeout="180" w="600" embed=true name="gesture" alt="an XY pad headed MOVE with the readout 2.0 s take and a rec button. Use `polar = true` when the value wraps around, like a phase or a hue. - Use `menu(...)` for choosing one of a few named options. - Use `gesture(...)` for a two-axis movement you want to perform once and loop. - For a curve over time you shape by hand, an envelope, use the keyframe editor, `keyframes(...)`: see [Keyframes and timelines](funFeatures.md#keyframes-and-timelines). It combines a waveform and native browser audio controls, keeps an optional vertical playhead synchronized with playback, and uses the waveform itself as a navigator: - click to seek; - drag to pan; - use the mouse wheel or `+` / `−` to zoom while keeping the visible playhead fixed on screen; - shift-wheel to pan; - double-click or press **all** to restore the complete clip. If the playhead is outside the visible interval, wheel zoom falls back to the pointer and button or keyboard zoom falls back to the center. Near the start or end of a recording, boundary clamping may move the playhead on screen. A completion-style spinner remains over the waveform while a newly zoomed or panned min/max envelope is loading, so the old waveform cannot be mistaken for the new view. During playback, crossing the right edge advances the visible interval and places the playhead slightly inside the new window; crossing the left edge after a backward seek mirrors that behavior. Set `followPlayhead = false` in `AudioVisualizerOptions` to keep a zoomed interval stationary. Waveform-envelope requests have a 15-second browser deadline; a stalled service clears the spinner and reports a timeout instead of leaving the view permanently busy. # Properties that re-run boxes A box can read a value that another box set. `prop(bpm)` in one box declares a typed property, `bpm`, that every box connected beneath it can read; the read walks up the box graph to the nearest box that has a value. That much is [property inheritance](running_code.md#property-inheritance-how-children-see-a-parents-values), and with plain `prop` nothing runs on its own: when the parent's value changes, a child sees the new value the next time *you* run the child. Swap `prop` for one of three variants and Field does the running for you: | Declare | What it adds | | --- | --- | | `propDown(name)` | Changing the value reruns every box that read it. | | `propUp(name)` | Reading a value nobody has set yet runs the box that sets it first. | | `propUpDown(name)` | Both. | Each declares the same inherited property `prop` does, read and written the same way. Only the re-running differs. Any of them can be assigned where it is declared, `propDown(bpm) = 120`, and any of them takes a default for when no box up the graph has a value yet: with `prop(runs, 0)`, a first `runs += 1` reads 0 rather than failing. `propUp` runs the supplier first and falls back to the default only if that still finds nothing. ## A change reruns the boxes that read it **Tempo** declares `bpm` with `propDown` and sets it: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} propDown(bpm) = 120 ``` **Beat** is connected beneath Tempo (select Tempo, then Beat, and press `g`). It reads `bpm` like any inherited property, and counts its own runs in a box property so we can see them: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/reactive_properties/beat.png" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait="1.5" timeout="180" embed=true name="reactive-props-beat" macro-file="../../dev_docs/agents/transcripts/docs_capture/reactive_props_down.yaml" capture-box="rp_beat" w="560" h="80" alt="Beat's main output, one line: bpm 90: a beat every 666 ms (run 2)"} prop(runs, 0) runs += 1 display("main", "

bpm $bpm: a beat every ${60000 / bpm} ms (run $runs)

") ``` Both boxes ran once. Then Tempo's code was changed to `propDown(bpm) = 90` and **only Tempo** was run. Beat says 90 and "run 2": the change reran it. What decides who reruns: - **Only boxes that read the value.** Field records which box read which property from whom (the record is kept with the document, in `dependencies.edn`, so it survives a restart). A box beneath Tempo that never reads `bpm` is left alone. - **Only a change.** Assigning the value it already has (by `equals`) reruns nothing. - **After the writing run.** A change made while Tempo runs waits until that run finishes, and is dropped if the run fails. A change made outside a run (a slider, a `frames {}` loop) goes at once. - **In dependency order, once each.** If Beat and a second box both read `bpm`, and a third reads from both of them, the third reruns once, after the other two. - **The writer's declaration decides.** Put `propDown` in the box that sets the value. A child that merely reads `bpm` gets the declaration from its parent and needs none of its own. A value changed every frame reruns its readers every frame. That is what `propDown` promises, but it is rarely what you want from a `frames {}` loop; keep such values in plain `prop`. ## A control reruns the boxes that read it A control bound with [`syncToProperty`](visualizers.md) writes into a box property. When that property is declared with `propDown`, moving the control reruns its readers, the same as an assignment in code. **Gain** declares `gain` and binds a slider to it: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/reactive_properties/gain.png" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait="1.5" timeout="180" embed=true name="reactive-props-gain" macro-file="../../dev_docs/agents/transcripts/docs_capture/reactive_props_slider.yaml" capture-box="rp_gain" w="560" h="80" alt="The Gain box with its controls panel open: one slider labelled GAIN, at 0.50 on a 0 to 1 track"} propDown(gain) syncToProperty("gain", 0.5, min = 0.0, max = 1.0) ``` **Meter**, beneath it, draws a bar `gain` long: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/reactive_properties/meter.png" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait="1.5" timeout="180" embed=true name="reactive-props-meter" macro-file="../../dev_docs/agents/transcripts/docs_capture/reactive_props_slider_drag.yaml" capture-box="rp_meter" w="560" h="80" alt="Meter's main output after Gain's slider is dragged most of the way up: a blue bar about 290 pixels long, and below it the text gain 0.97"} val width = (gain * 300).toInt() display("main", "

gain ${"%.2f".format(gain)}

") ``` Drag Gain's slider and Meter redraws as you go; there is no need to run Meter yourself. ??? aside "Agents: the slider capture" Meter's capture is taken after a real pointer drag of Gain's slider (`reactive_props_slider_drag.yaml`), which fails if the slider does not move. `ReactivePropsTest.aRawWriteToADeclaredDownPropertyIsAChange` pins the control's write as a change. ## A missing value runs its supplier `propDown` covers a value that changes. `propUp` covers a value that is not there yet: you open a document and run a box near the bottom of a chain before the boxes above it. **Scale** sets `scale` and counts its runs: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} propUp(scale) scale = 2.5 prop(runs, 0) runs += 1 ``` **Plot**, beneath it, also declares `propUp(scale)`, and only Plot is run: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/reactive_properties/plot.png" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait="1.5" timeout="180" embed=true name="reactive-props-plot" macro-file="../../dev_docs/agents/transcripts/docs_capture/reactive_props_up.yaml" capture-box="rp_plot" w="560" h="80" alt="Plot's main output, one line: scale = 2.5 (Scale has run 1 time)"} propUp(scale) prop(runs, 0) val s = scale val ran = thisBox.named("Scale").runs display("main", "

scale = $s (Scale has run $ran time)

") ``` Plot's read of `scale` found nothing, ran Scale *inside the read*, waited for it, and carried on with 2.5. While a pull runs, other boxes' `frames {}` loops and a native graphics window keep advancing. A supplier that blocks the thread (`Thread.sleep`, a busy loop) blocks everything for as long as it blocks. `propUpDown` is both: a missing value runs its supplier, and a changed one reruns its readers. `rootPropUp`, `rootPropDown` and `rootPropUpDown` do the same for a document-wide `rootProp` slot, read and written as `root.name`; the box whose code declares it is the supplier. ## Seeing who reads what The palette's **Toggle Dependency Layer** draws, over the canvas, one arrow from each box that supplied a value to each box that read it, labelled with the names that flowed. The dependency layer draws an arrow from Tempo to Beat labelled bpm, one from Tempo to Harmony labelled key, and one from Tempo past Beat to Accent labelled with both names; the recent reads are amber, the older blue. The grey connection lines of the box graph run beneath them."} ui.eval("window.toggleDependencyLayer(); localStorage.setItem('afield.dependencyLayer', '0'); return true") for (i in 0 until 40) { ui.pause(250) if ((ui.eval("return window.dependencyLayerState().drawnPaths").toString().toDoubleOrNull() ?: 0.0) >= 3.0) break } ui.pause(500) ``` Accent's arrow starts at Tempo, not at Beat: an inherited value comes from the box that holds it, however many levels up. An arrow is bright (amber) for a couple of seconds after a read, solid for a read seen since Field started, and faint and dashed for one only remembered from an earlier session. A read that found nothing puts a red `? name` tag on the reader. **Clear Dependency Record** forgets what the document has recorded. ## Seeing what ran `ReactiveRuns.recentEvents()` lists every start, end, pull and cascade, in order. scale = $s (Scale has run $ran time)

") ``` Plot's read of `scale` found nothing, ran Scale *inside the read*, waited for it, and carried on with 2.5. A chain unwinds the same way: a leaf that reads from B, which reads from A, runs B, which runs A, in that order, each once. - **The reader declares it.** Up is decided by the reading box's declaration. A box that only reads a parent's `propUp` value compiles against the parent's declaration even before the parent has run. - **Which box supplies it.** The box asked, then the box whose declaration the reader inherited, then boxes that supplied the name before, then any ancestor whose code declares it, nearest first. - **A value that is present is just read.** Nothing runs when the walk finds a value. - **Cycles fail.** If A's read pulls B and B's read needs A, the read fails and the message names the cycle. While a pull runs, other boxes' `frames {}` loops and a native graphics window keep advancing. A supplier that blocks the thread (`Thread.sleep`, a busy loop) blocks everything for as long as it blocks. `propUpDown` is both: a missing value runs its supplier, and a changed one reruns its readers. `rootPropUp`, `rootPropDown` and `rootPropUpDown` do the same for a document-wide `rootProp` slot, read and written as `root.name`; the box whose code declares it is the supplier. ## Seeing who reads what The palette's **Toggle Dependency Layer** draws, over the canvas, one arrow from each box that supplied a value to each box that read it, labelled with the names that flowed.
